# The Repair Line as Language Infrastructure

**Aim.** Avenki is heard in Marrowport’s publicly owned housing towers but is largely absent from maintenance systems, where tenants must use Dorran. This project asks whether allowing residents to request essential repairs in Avenki increases everyday language use and improves service parity. It tests preservation as civic utility, not only cultural documentation.

**Design.** Over 18 months, 12 towers—about 240 households—will enter a stepped-wedge pilot at three-month intervals. Each receives an Avenki voice-note and text channel staffed by paid bilingual residents, while existing Dorran routes remain available. Before and after rollout, researchers will collect channel choice, acknowledgement and repair times, repeat use, and code-switching rates. Surveys and interviews with adolescents, adults, and elders will examine confidence using Avenki for technical matters and whether repair vocabulary travels between generations. Not-yet-enrolled towers provide contemporaneous comparisons; models will adjust for building condition and request type.

**Outputs and governance.** With separate consent, selected requests will feed a community-owned glossary for plumbing, heating, and electrical faults. A tenant council will set access rules, approve quotations, and may withhold terms judged private or politically risky. Participants will be paid; raw audio will be deleted after 30 days; immigration status will not be collected. The city housing office will receive aggregate findings only.

**Evaluation.** The primary outcome is the share of requests made partly or wholly in Avenki six months after launch. Secondary outcomes are service-time gaps and self-reported cross-generational vocabulary use. Rollout order will follow operational readiness rather than random assignment, so causal estimates may retain selection bias. Additional bilingual staffing may itself speed repairs, making language access hard to isolate. Eighteen months also cannot establish long-term language survival. Even so, the study can show whether an essential public service becomes a practical site of linguistic participation rather than another pressure to assimilate.
planted_strengths: Uses a distinctive, policy-relevant angle by treating an essential housing service as language infrastructure rather than focusing only on archives or schooling.
Provides a feasible mixed-methods design with a comparison strategy, defined primary and secondary outcomes, and attention to service equity.
Includes meaningful community governance, participant payment, restricted institutional access, data minimization, and separate consent for glossary creation.
Acknowledges major threats to causal inference and avoids claiming that a short pilot can prove long-term language preservation.
Connects linguistic participation to unequal access to public services without using inflammatory or demeaning framing.
planted_weaknesses: The non-random rollout based on operational readiness creates selection bias that statistical adjustment may not adequately address.
The intervention bundles language access with additional bilingual staffing, preventing clean attribution of faster repairs or increased participation to language choice alone.
The primary outcome measures short-term use of a service channel, which is only an indirect proxy for language preservation.
The proposal gives no power calculation, recruitment plan, attrition strategy, or detail on how code-switching will be measured reliably.
An 18-month study in 12 housing towers has limited capacity to assess durable intergenerational transmission or support generalization beyond public housing.
quality_rationale: The proposal is focused, original, ethically attentive, and methodologically more concrete than a typical short research idea. Its civic-service framing gives minority-language preservation tangible political stakes, while the stepped-wedge structure and mixed outcomes provide a credible basis for inquiry. However, the bundled intervention, non-random rollout, underspecified analysis details, and weak connection between short-term channel use and long-term preservation materially limit the conclusions. These visible rough edges support a good but not excellent score.
title: The Repair Line as Language Infrastructure
topic: Testing whether minority-language access to public-housing repair systems strengthens everyday use, intergenerational technical vocabulary, and service equity.
